extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, legal counsel for educational institutions and other Title IX recipients, civil rights stakeholders, and policy readers
extracted.subtask_description: Department of Education final regulations and explanatory discussion interpreting §106.31(a)(2) and related Title IX provisions, focused on gender identity, parental rights, religious exemptions, appearance codes, health-care intersections, and juvenile facilities. Provides legal standards, statutory interpretation, and examples/case citations for recipients of federal education funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on policies preventing participation consistent with gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.31(a)(2) prohibits a recipient from adopting a policy or engaging in a practice that prevents a person from participating in an education program or activity consistent with the person's gender identity when that person seeks to participate consistent with their gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals (and parents, as appropriate) are better positioned to weigh harms and benefits for themselves than an educational institution. Recipients retain discretion to provide sex‑separate facilities consistent with Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate; the prohibition targets policies/practices that bar participation consistent with gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis harm standard for sex‑separate facilities and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations bar treating or separating students on the basis of sex in a manner that causes more than de minimis harm (as reflected in §106.31(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making explicit protections against sex‑based harms does not eliminate permissible sex‑separate arrangements; recipients may still provide sex‑separate facilities consistent with nondiscrimination. See the discussion of the de minimis harm standard (Section IV.B.1) and case law cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections apply to all students (not limited to transgender students)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) is not limited to transgender students and protects all students from harm when a recipient separates or treats students differently based on sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department notes it is unaware of instances where cisgender students excluded from facilities inconsistent with their gender identity experienced the same harms transgender students experience; nevertheless the protection is not limited in wording to any subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidentiary presumption that transgender presence creates safety/privacy risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagrees that transgender students inherently pose safety risks or that their mere presence in single‑sex spaces compromises others' privacy interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are unsubstantiated or generalized, courts have rejected them (cases cited: Grimm, Whitaker, Boyertown, Parents for Priv., Cruzan). The Supreme Court has also rejected discomfort of some as a justification for discrimination (City of Cleburne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may offer but are not required to provide gender‑neutral or single‑occupancy facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in Title IX or the final regulations prevents a recipient from offering single‑occupancy or gender‑neutral facilities to students seeking additional privacy, but the Department declines to require recipients to provide them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such facilities may be helpful accommodations, but they are not the only way to provide nondiscriminatory access; requirement would have cost implications and would warrant public comment before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients can adopt nondiscriminatory privacy/safety measures without excluding transgender students
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in §106.31(a)(2) prohibits recipients from taking nondiscriminatory steps to ensure privacy and safety for all students in sex‑separate facilities (e.g., rules prohibiting harassment, assault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may make and enforce rules protecting privacy and safety that apply to all students and do not exclude transgender students from accessing facilities consistent with their gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX 'living facilities' carve‑out limited to housing (20 U.S.C. 1686)
rubrics_metrics.description: 20 U.S.C. 1686 permits educational institutions to maintain separate living facilities for different sexes; that carve‑out applies only to living facilities and does not permit subjecting persons to more than de minimis harm in other contexts (e.g., bathrooms, locker rooms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The housing carve‑out provides the statutory basis for §106.32(b)(1). Other facilities (toilets, locker rooms, showers) are governed by the general nondiscrimination mandate (20 U.S.C. 1681) and §106.33; the Department rejects reasoning (e.g., Adams) that would extend the housing carve‑out to those contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.31(a)(2) does not bar recipients from voluntarily allowing access to sex‑separate housing consistent with gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the express carve‑out for sex‑separate living facilities under 20 U.S.C. 1686, §106.31(a)(2) does not prohibit a recipient from excluding or allowing students access to sex‑separate housing consistent with their gender identity; recipients may voluntarily choose policies enabling access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies the reach: the housing carve‑out is limited and does not give recipients license to cause more than de minimis harm outside housing contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental rights preserved; §106.6(g) reinforces parental authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations disturbs parental rights; §106.6(g) reinforces a parent's right to act on behalf of their minor child (including making complaints through grievance procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parents and minor students disagree, deference to a parent/guardian authorized to act on behalf of the minor is appropriate. Recipients can coordinate with minor students and parents to ensure equal access. See §§106.44(j)(2), 106.6(g) discussions for disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may disclose information about minors to parents with legal right to receive it
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from disclosing information about a minor child to their parent who has the legal right to receive disclosures on behalf of their child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See discussions of §§106.44(j) and 106.6(g) for additional explanation of information disclosure to parents of minor children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' Title IX obligations are not obviated by state or local law
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.6(b) affirms that a recipient's obligation to comply with Title IX and the regulations is not obviated or alleviated by any State or local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department declines to opine generally on conflicts with specific state laws without a fact‑specific analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will not regulate curricula under Title IX (34 CFR 106.42)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not have authority to regulate curricula; the final regulations do not regulate curricular materials or instructional choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit regulatory limitation: 'Nothing in this regulation shall be interpreted as requiring or prohibiting or abridging in any way the use of particular textbooks or curricular materials.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'parental status' limited in scope and does not alter parental rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of 'in loco parentis' in the definition of 'parental status' is limited to certain provisions (e.g., §§106.21(c)(2)(i), 106.37(a)(3), 106.40(a), 106.57(a)(1)) and does not affect parental rights, authorize a recipient to act in place of parents, or diminish parental rights under §106.6(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That definition relates to prohibitions on discrimination related to parental status (e.g., treating mothers less favorably than fathers) and does not bestow parental authority on any person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX coverage of institutional health‑care operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient is an educational institution, all of its operations — including campus health centers, teaching hospitals, and nurses' offices — are part of the covered 'education program or activity' and thus subject to Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non‑educational recipients, Title IX applies only to any education program or activity they operate. Citations include Public Law 100‑259 and DOJ Title IX Legal Manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX regulations do not create medical standards or require specific medical treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's Title IX regulations do not (and cannot) promote any particular medical treatment, require provision of particular medical procedures, or set any standard of care; they implement nondiscrimination requirements and do not interfere with providers' professional medical judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about medical standards of care (e.g., requiring gender‑affirming care) are beyond Title IX's scope. Overlaps with HHS Section 1557 exist but are addressed in separate rulemaking; Department will collaborate with other agencies as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech and RFRA protections preserved in enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.6(d) states that nothing in the regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights protected under the First Amendment; the Department must act in accordance with the Constitution and consider RFRA when evaluating compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cannot predict RFRA outcomes in hypothetical cases; evaluation of RFRA claims is fact‑specific. Individuals may notify the Department about RFRA burdens (RFRA@ed.gov). The religious exemption for institutions is separately available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious exemption for educational institutions controlled by religious organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: §§106.10 and 106.31(a)(2) do not apply to an educational institution controlled by a religious organization to the extent that application would be inconsistent with the religious tenets of that organization (per 20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An institution seeking to claim an exemption should have its highest‑ranking official submit a written statement to the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights identifying the conflicting Title IX provisions (34 CFR 106.12(b)). The exemption applies to institutions/entities, not to individuals' exercise of religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and dress/grooming codes are subject to Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex‑specific appearance codes, including dress and grooming codes, are subject to Title IX and §106.31(a)(2); a recipient may adopt sex‑based distinctions only to the extent those distinctions do not cause more than de minimis harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some sex‑based distinctions may be appropriate (e.g., protective gear, uniforms in PE or athletics). Imposing different restrictions on how boys and girls dress or appear can violate Title IX if it causes more than de minimis harm. Historical regulatory changes (1975 inclusion, 1982 removal) do not create an exemption from Title IX; courts (e.g., Peltier, Hayden, Arnold) have recognized coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable‑burdens or 'equal burdens' defense rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient cannot defend a sex‑specific appearance code by arguing that it imposes 'comparable' or 'equal' burdens on both sexes; Title IX protects individuals of both sexes equally and discrimination against both does not eliminate liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites Bostock and Peltier for the proposition that discriminating against members of both sexes does not eliminate liability but 'doubles it.' The Department is aware some courts still apply a 'comparable burdens' test but disagrees with that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to juvenile justice facilities limited to education programs; PREA concerns addressed case‑by‑case
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX regulations apply to juvenile justice facilities that receive Department funds only with respect to education programs or activities they offer. §106.31(a)(2) does not apply where different treatment causing more than de minimis harm is permitted by Title IX (e.g., living facilities under 20 U.S.C. 1686).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes juvenile facilities' obligations under PREA (28 CFR 115.311) but finds generalized anecdotal evidence insufficient to show these regulations will increase risk of sexual assault. Fact‑specific analysis may be required in particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should coordinate with minors and parents to ensure equal access
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient can coordinate with a minor student and their parent, as appropriate, to ensure sex discrimination does not interfere with the student's equal access to its education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical coordination is encouraged; specific factual scenarios require case‑by‑case determinations. See §§106.44(j)(2) and 106.6(g) for additional disclosure and procedural guidance.
